Kaunas Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Kauno apskritis, Lithuania

Not demolished. Some of Kaunas's earliest Jews may have arrived as Crimean prisoners brought by Grand Duke Vytautas the Great in the late 14th century; the community endured repeated cycles of expulsion and restricted resettlement over the following centuries — commemorated locally each year on Shushan Purim through a reading called the Kowno Megillah — before finally gaining permission to buy cemetery land within Kaunas itself in 1862. By 1897 Jews were a relative majority of the city, and after Kaunas became the capital of independent Lithuania in 1923, its Jewish community supported roughly 40 synagogues and yeshivot, two theaters, and several newspapers. In 1939, the Japanese vice-consul Chiune Sugihara issued transit visas that saved an estimated 6,000 Jewish refugees who had fled to Kaunas. After the German invasion of 1941, nearly 30,000 Jews were confined in the Kaunas ghetto at Slobodka, and the Ninth Fort became a major site of mass murder; by July 1944, retreating forces fire-bombed every house in the ghetto, killing about 1,500 people hiding in bunkers, with only 90 escaping. A separate Jewish cemetery in Slobodka was destroyed by Soviet authorities in 1963, though this cemetery survived and remains fenced and protected today.
